newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia PM vote adjourned until Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia PM vote adjourned until Thursday.

text.p: Janez Drnovsek on Wednesday appealed to parliament to back him for a second term as Slovenia's prime minister after a defector from a rightwing party offered him a vital one-vote margin in parliament.
The parliamentary session and vote on Drnovsek's mandate to form a government was adjourned until 10 a.m. (0900 GMT) on Thursday as a debate dragged on into the evening.
Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats won 25 of parliament's 90 seats in a November general election, which was Slovenia's second since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
During two months of negotiations, Drnovsek, who was president of Yugoslavia from 1989 to 1990, secured 20 votes from smaller parties, including the former communists.
But an absolute majority of 46 appeared to elude him until Ciril Pucko defected from the Christian Democrats on Wednesday.

"I am here to ask you for your support in the election for leader of a new government," Drnovsek told parliament earlier in a pre-vote address. "I am sure that you will decide according to your conscience and with your full responsibilities to Slovenia's citizens."

Defending his economic record during four years in power, Drnovsek said he would strive to secure economic growth of between four and five percent a year and cut inflation to at least four percent from the current rate of nine percent.
Pucko's defection infuriated an alliance of three rightwing parties that had been confident of preventing Drnovsek from returning to power.

The alliance, comprising the conservative People's Party, the centre-right Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats, had won 45 seats in the election, and also needed one extra vote for an absolute majority.

Social Democrat leader Janez Jansa, a former defence minister who helped organise Slovenia's fight against Yugoslav federal troops in 1991, accused Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats of bribing Pucko for his support.
"We are not surprised (by the defection)...because the Liberal Democrats had already tried to bribe several of our deputies," Jansa told Slovenian television.
"Liberal democracy is based on corruption which is a very weak foundation. I do not believe this government will have any success," he added.
Jansa warned that Drnovsek would not be able to secure the necessary two-thirds majority in parliament he would need to change the constitution for membership of the European Union.
Drnovsek, a committed pro-European, had crowned his four years in power by signing an association agreement with the EU, vowing to reform the economy before planned entry in 2001.
The agreement with the EU hinged on Slovenia changing its laws to enable foreigners to buy real estate -- which the rightwing alliance could now technically block.
